questions.stimulusText:
My task was simple: get everyone looking at the camera at the same time. I straightened shoulders, shifted a chair, and asked my cousin Selby to stop balancing on one foot. For a moment we were a shelf of upright books.
My aunt set the camera to take its photograph after ten seconds and hurried into the row. Grandfather Rosh had left his straw hat on the table. Nobody was supposed to move now.
Then the garden door blew open. A draft lifted the hat, tipped it over the table's edge, and sent it rolling across the floor. Selby broke formation and caught it. Instead of putting it back, she placed it askew on her head.
Grandfather began to laugh. My aunt bent forward to see what had happened. I turned to restore order, but Selby saluted me beneath the enormous brim, and I laughed too. The camera clicked while my eyes were nearly closed.
Later, we examined the photographs. In the earlier ones, every face was visible and every shoulder was straight. In the last, Grandfather's hand rested on Selby's shoulder, my aunt leaned into the group, and nobody looked directly at the lens.
"I failed," I said.
Grandfather chose the last photograph. "This one has all of us."
The others did too, of course. But I knew he was not counting faces.

questions.prompt: Under the passage's equal-wheel assumption, why must the outside wheel make more revolutions during a turn?

choices.A: It completes the turn in a longer time than the inside wheel.
choices.B: It follows a longer path, while each revolution covers the same distance for either wheel.
choices.C: Its circumference automatically becomes larger during every turn.
choices.D: The inside wheel must stop moving whenever the cart changes direction.

questions.correctAnswer: It follows a longer path, while each revolution covers the same distance for either wheel.
questions.explanation: The passage combines a longer outside path with equal circumferences, so the outside wheel must rotate more times in the shared interval.
questions.stimulusText:
Imagine a cart with two wheels of equal size on the same axle. On a straight path, both wheels travel equal distances. During a turn, however, the outside wheel must traverse a longer path than the inside wheel. Both complete the turn in the same time, so equal-sized wheels need different rotation rates if each is to roll without sliding.
Each full revolution of a wheel carries it forward by one circumference. The longer outside path therefore calls for more revolutions. A solid connection that forces both wheels to rotate at exactly the same rate prevents this difference. One wheel may then drag or slip rather than roll smoothly along its own path.
A differential is a mechanism that allows the two connected wheels to turn at different rates while receiving power. In this simplified account, its importance is not that it always makes one wheel faster. It allows a difference when the paths require one. During straight travel, equal rotation rates can still be appropriate.
The model depends on its assumptions. In particular, the wheels have equal circumferences. If their sizes differed, counting revolutions alone would no longer directly compare the distances traveled. The explanation links the shape of the route to wheel motion by keeping wheel size and elapsed time fixed, rather than treating a turn as though both wheels followed the same track.

questions.stimulusTitle: An Imaginary Case, a Real Question
questions.stimulusText:
Two people want to share a coil of twine and a hammock. "Cut everything into equal halves," one proposes. The twine can become two usable lengths. Cutting the hammock down the middle, however, would not produce two working hammocks. The same physical procedure has different consequences for what the objects allow people to do.
This invented case is a thought experiment. It does not describe an actual disagreement or predict how particular neighbors will behave. Instead, it tests an attractive rule by making one distinction easy to examine. Dividing material equally is not always the same as sharing its benefit. Leaving other details out can isolate that distinction.
The missing details still matter if anyone wants a practical decision. The case says nothing about who already owns the objects. Nor does it explain whether both people need long pieces of twine or whether they could take turns using the hammock. Adding such facts might change the preferred arrangement without erasing the distinction the example revealed.
A useful thought experiment therefore makes its conditions clear and acknowledges what it leaves unsettled. Its simplicity can expose an assumption that ordinary discussion overlooks. That is a reason to use the imaginary case carefully, rather than either dismiss it for being invented or treat it as a complete answer to every real dispute. It is a question directed at a principle, not a verdict on unknown people.

choices.B: whether she can become an apprentice
choices.C: when the brass weight was manufactured

questions.explanation: The opening paragraph identifies the workshop's promise to respond to her apprenticeship request; the later household details are distractions from that answer.
questions.stimulusText:
Neri laid the unopened envelope beside the brass weight on her desk. The roofers' workshop had promised to write about her request to become an apprentice. Now its answer was here, and she was polishing a weight that had not needed polishing yesterday.
"Not yet," she told the envelope.
She carried a cup to the kitchen. She returned a borrowed ruler. At the window she watched rain gather on a wire until one drop grew heavy enough to fall. The envelope waited without becoming either thinner or kinder.
Her brother came in looking for string. "Have you heard?"
"They've written."
He reached toward the desk, then stopped when she put her hand over the envelope. "You want me to leave?"
She had expected him to laugh at her waiting. His question gave her nothing to resist. She nodded, and he went out carrying the string.
Neri lifted the brass weight. Under it, the corner of the envelope had made a pale, clean triangle in the dust. She had spent the morning moving everything except the one thing that mattered.
Outside, another drop loosened from the wire. She slid a finger beneath the flap.
The room looked exactly as it had a moment before. She was glad of that. Whatever the letter said, she would read it in this room, standing on these boards, with the same rain at the window.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what allows graphite layers to slide?

choices.A: The attraction between sheets is weaker than the bonds within a sheet.
choices.B: Graphite contains no bonds between any of its atoms.
choices.C: Each sheet is made from a different chemical element.

questions.stimulusText:
Graphite and diamond can both consist of carbon, yet they behave very differently. Graphite can leave a dark mark when drawn across paper. Diamond is extremely hard. The contrast cannot be explained simply by saying that one contains carbon and the other does not.
The arrangement of the carbon atoms matters. In graphite, atoms are strongly bonded within sheets. The attraction between those sheets is much weaker, allowing layers to slide and small pieces to rub off. A pencil mark therefore does not show that every bond in graphite is weak. It reveals a difference between the connections within a layer and the connections between layers.
In diamond, each carbon atom is bonded to neighboring atoms in a three-dimensional network. There is no equivalent stack of easily sliding sheets. The network helps explain why diamond resists scratching. Hardness here describes resistance to scratching, not a guarantee that a material can never break.
These structures show why identifying an element is only part of describing a material. Two samples can have the same kind of atom while differing in the way those atoms are connected. To understand a property, a useful question is not only "What is it made of?" but also "How is it put together?" Neither question replaces the other; the two descriptions work together.

questions.prompt: What do the groups share in the round described?

choices.A: the same starting instant
choices.B: a requirement to sing at different speeds
choices.C: a rule that only one group may sing at a time
choices.D: the same melody

questions.correctAnswer: the same melody
questions.explanation: The opening defines a round as groups singing the same melody with different starting times, separating shared musical material from staggered entrances.
questions.stimulusText:
When singers perform a melody in unison, they sing its corresponding notes together. A round uses a different plan: groups sing the same melody but begin at different times. One group may be several measures into the tune when the next group enters at its beginning.
The delay does not necessarily mean that one group sings more slowly. With a common pace, the groups can maintain their separation as they proceed. Because different portions sound simultaneously, the combined texture differs from the single line heard at the opening. A melody chosen for a round must work with its own overlapping portions; not every tune produces a satisfying combination when entrances are staggered.
This overlap distinguishes a round from a simple echo in which groups take turns repeating a phrase, with only one group singing at a time. Both involve repetition, but only the described round has different portions of the same melody sounding together. Repetition alone is therefore not enough to identify the arrangement.
A written plan can make the timing visible. Imagine identical horizontal rows of notes shifted to the right for later entrances. Reading one row follows a group's melody through time. Looking straight down the rows at a particular moment shows what the groups are singing together. The tune belongs to each row; the texture depends on how those rows align. Listening to a round involves hearing both at once.

The customs clerk looked up from a stack of papers. "You've come for the seal?"
"Yes. Will it fit in here?" Beto raised the pail.
The clerk considered him for a moment, then opened a drawer. From it she lifted a brass stamp scarcely longer than her thumb. She pressed it into a patch of soft wax on an envelope. Its impression showed a ship above three waves.
Beto studied the fish. The clerk studied the pail.
"Very considerate," she said, putting the stamp into his empty hand. "But this one has never asked for lunch."

questions.prompt: In the first example, how many tokens does Mila pay after bidding nine?

choices.A: nine
choices.B: four
choices.C: seven
choices.D: eleven

questions.correctAnswer: seven

questions.stimulusTitle: A Price Set by Another Bid
questions.stimulusText:
A fictional token auction separates the amount that wins from the amount the winner pays. Each bidder secretly writes one bid. The highest bidder receives the object but pays the second-highest bid. Only the winner pays. The examples here have no tied bids.
Suppose Mila bids nine tokens, Ren bids seven, and Tess bids four. Mila wins and pays seven tokens. Her bid determines her ranking, but Ren's bid sets her price. If Mila had bid eleven while the others kept their bids, she would still win and still pay seven. Raising an already winning bid would not, in that example, raise the payment.
That does not make a bid meaningless or guarantee that higher bidding is harmless. Suppose Mila is willing to spend no more than six tokens for the object but bids nine anyway. Against Ren's seven, she wins and must pay more than she wanted. If she bids six instead, Ren wins, so Mila does not incur a payment.
The rule therefore gives a bid two connected roles. It helps determine whether someone wins, while the other bids determine the price that a winner must accept. To understand a bidder's result, asking only "What did that person offer?" is insufficient. One must also examine the competing bids and the payment rule.

questions.prompt: In the chair example, what must the walker do while keeping a face toward the chair for a full circuit?

choices.A: remain facing the same wall throughout
choices.B: avoid turning the body at every position
choices.C: make one complete turn relative to the room
choices.D: walk only halfway around the chair

questions.correctAnswer: make one complete turn relative to the room
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states that continuously facing the chair requires gradual turning, totaling one complete turn relative to the room after a circuit.
questions.stimulusText:
The Moon presents approximately the same face toward Earth as it travels around our planet. Two mistaken conclusions can follow: that the Moon does not rotate, or that its far side must remain without sunlight. Neither conclusion follows from the observation.
To examine rotation, imagine walking around a chair while keeping your face toward it. At each new position, you must turn your body slightly. After one complete circuit, your body has made one complete turn relative to the room. If instead you keep facing one fixed wall throughout the circuit, you will face the chair at some positions and turn your back to it at others.
The Moon similarly rotates once during each trip around Earth, keeping roughly the same side directed toward us. The imagined walker is an explanatory device: it separates turning about one's own center from traveling around another object. The two motions can occur together, with their periods matched.
Illumination is a different question. The far side is called far because it faces away from Earth, not because sunlight never reaches it. As the Moon moves and turns, different portions receive sunlight. Being hidden from an Earthbound observer does not mean being permanently unlit.
This motion model explains how a familiar view can coexist with rotation. It does not explain the history of how the periods became matched; describing an arrangement and explaining its development are separate tasks.

questions.stimulusText:
An invented poem ends, "The last stitch carries the seam." In its context, the image suggests that careful finishing secures earlier work. A translator faces more than a choice between replacing each word and inventing an unrelated message.
One rendering keeps the stitch and seam, preserving the compact image but leaving an unfamiliar reader to interpret it. Another says, "Finish carefully so earlier work holds." That version makes the implied advice explicit but removes the sewing image. Both retain a central claim while producing different reading experiences.
A brief note could explain the image without replacing it. Yet the note adds a pause that the original line may not have required. Its usefulness depends partly on the audience: readers exploring an unfamiliar poem may welcome that help, while readers following a song may prefer an uninterrupted line.
These choices do not make every version equally faithful. A sentence claiming that finishing never matters would reverse the poem's idea. That is a change in the claim, not merely a different balance between image and explanation.
To evaluate the work, a critic should therefore identify what the translation is trying to preserve and ask whether its choices achieve that purpose without reversing the original meaning. Keeping imagery, clarifying an implication, and maintaining a reading rhythm are related aims, but they are not interchangeable tests.
